Snapchat Scam UK: Fake Messages & Impersonation

Scammers are using Snapchat to impersonate the company itself, steal login details, and run money-flipping and romance fraud schemes.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-08-18 · 8 min read

Quick answer: Snapchat itself does not ask for passwords, payment details, or personal ID via message. If you receive such a request, it is a scam. Do not reply or click links. Report the account to Snapchat and block the sender immediately.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

What Snapchat scams look like

Four patterns cover most of what turns up. The most common is a fake verification message: your account has been locked or flagged, and you need to confirm your password, email or payment details to sort it out. Romance fraud works slowly, with the scammer building a relationship over weeks or months before the first request for money, usually for an emergency, travel or a business opportunity. Money-flipping schemes offer to double whatever you send first. Other accounts simply pose as Snapchat support and charge a fee to unlock an account or restore deleted photos.

All of it leans on disappearing messages, which delete after viewing and can make a conversation harder to evidence. Less survives than you would like, but not nothing. Snap says a report made from inside the app can include the reported chat and the messages sent just before it, so report from the conversation rather than assuming it has already gone. Scammers often go after younger users, who are less likely to know how the real Snapchat behaves.

How to spot a Snapchat scam message

  • The message asks for your password, email address, phone number or payment card details. Snapchat's own guidance on password safety says its representatives will never need your password.
  • Your account is supposedly locked, suspended or flagged, and you must act now. A real lock shows up when you try to log in through the app, not as a message from another account.
  • You are asked to click a link to verify your identity or log in again. Snapchat does not send you login links inside Snapchat.
  • Someone offers to unlock your account, restore deleted content or boost your followers for a fee. None of those are Snapchat services.
  • A contact you barely know needs money for an emergency, an investment or travel. That is a romance or advance-fee scam.
  • The sender says they are from Snapchat support. Support does not open a conversation with you out of the blue, so reach it yourself from Settings inside the app or from Snapchat's help site.
  • You are pushed to carry on the conversation somewhere else, on WhatsApp, Telegram or Instagram. That gets you away from Snapchat's own reporting tools.

How the scam unfolds from first contact

It starts either with a direct message from an account you do not know, or with something that looks like it came from Snapchat. In the fake verification version, your account supposedly needs urgent attention, and the message carries a link or instructions to log in. The link leads to a login page that looks like Snapchat and belongs to the scammer, who captures whatever you type the moment you type it.

Romance scams take longer. The scammer sets up a fake profile, often with stolen photos, and chats to you for weeks or months until the trust is there. Then comes the problem: a flight to visit you, medical bills, a business investment, a debt to clear. Payment is by bank transfer, gift cards or cryptocurrency. Money-flipping runs faster and cruder, with screenshots of supposed earnings and a promise to multiply whatever you send. Either way, once the money moves, they go.

Disappearing messages make all of this harder to evidence afterwards, which is part of why scammers like the app. They do not wipe the slate, though. Snap says an in-app report can carry the reported chat and the messages immediately before it, so report from inside the conversation, and screenshot what you can while you can.

How to check if a message is really from Snapchat

Do not try to judge whether the account messaging you is really Snapchat. Go to support yourself and the question stops mattering. Open Snapchat, tap your profile icon, open the settings gear and choose Support, which takes you into Snapchat's own help centre.

Snapchat's published guidance on keeping your password safe is explicit that its representatives will never need your password. A message asking you to confirm one is a scam, however official it looks, and the same goes for any message asking you to verify your account or hand over payment details. Do not reply and do not click anything. Report the account instead: open the message, tap the three dots and choose Report.

If you are unsure whether your account has a real problem, log out completely and log back in through the official app. A genuine lock shows up at that point rather than in a message from another user, and Snapchat's own account-lock guidance sets out the recovery routes from there.

What to do if you have already sent money or shared details

For a bank transfer, phone your bank now and tell them you have been defrauded. Ask them to try to recall the payment. An eligible payment sent by Faster Payments or CHAPS from a UK account on or after 7 October 2024 may also be covered by the mandatory reimbursement rules for authorised push payment fraud: you have 13 months to claim, reimbursement is capped at £85,000, exclusions apply, and your firm may deduct an excess of up to £100, though it cannot take that excess from a consumer it assesses as vulnerable.

Ask the bank to assess the claim and to tell you what evidence it needs.

Gift cards and cryptocurrency are harder, because those payments rarely reverse. Report it anyway to the platform you bought them from, which may be able to freeze the receiving account.

Shared your password, email address or phone number? Change your Snapchat password from a device the scammer has never touched, then turn on two-factor authentication for Snapchat and for the email account behind it. Check your recent logins for anything you did not do. If bank details or a card number went across, ask your bank to watch the account.

Where you are worried about your identity being misused, the UK mechanism is Cifas Protective Registration. It costs £30, runs for two years, and asks lenders to carry out extra checks before granting credit in your name. Apply at cifas.org.uk/pr. You can also request your statutory credit report free of charge from the agencies MoneyHelper lists, Experian, Equifax and TransUnion, the three main ones, plus Crediva, and read it for accounts you never opened.

How to report a Snapchat scam in the UK

Report the account to Snapchat first: open the message, tap the three dots and choose Report. Snap says reports are reviewed against its Community Guidelines and can lead to enforcement action on the account, which may mean a warning, a restriction or removal.

Then report the scam itself, and the route depends on where you live. In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, report it to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 or at https://www.reportfraud.police.uk. In Scotland, report it to Police Scotland on 101 or through https://www.scotland.police.uk/contact-us/non-emergencies/.

A fake login page, or any other suspicious website, goes to the National Cyber Security Centre through its report a suspicious website form at https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/section/about-this-website/report-scam-website. Its Suspicious Email Reporting Service mailbox is a separate route for suspicious emails and is not the place for a website. A scam text goes somewhere else again: forward it to 7726, the shortcode run by the mobile networks.

For advice rather than reporting, the consumer helplines are Citizens Advice on 0808 223 1133 in England and Wales, Advice Direct Scotland on 0808 800 9060 in Scotland, and Consumerline on 0300 123 6262 in Northern Ireland. Keep the scammer's username, the dates and times, and any screenshots you took before the messages went.

Frequently asked questions

Is a message asking me to verify my Snapchat account real?

No. Snapchat does not ask you to verify your account via direct message. If your account has a genuine issue, you will see a notification when you log in through the official app, or you can check your account settings. Any message asking you to click a link or provide your password is a scam. Report the account and block the sender.

Someone on Snapchat is asking me to send money. Are they real?

Almost certainly not. Scammers build a friendship or a relationship on Snapchat first, then ask for money for an emergency, travel or an investment. Anyone you have known a short time who starts asking for money is running a scam. Send nothing, block them, and report the account to Snapchat.

I clicked a link in a Snapchat message and entered my password. What should I do?

Change your Snapchat password immediately from a different device. Enable two-factor authentication on your Snapchat account and on the email address linked to it. Monitor your account for any unauthorised activity. If the link also asked for your email or phone number, change the password on those accounts too and check for any suspicious activity.

Can Snapchat recover my account if a scammer has taken it over?

Act quickly. Report the account as hacked through Snapchat's support page, in the app or on the web, and give them whatever identifying detail you have: username, email, phone number. Snapchat's own account-lock guidance sets out the recovery routes from there. Change your password as soon as you get back in.

What should I do if I sent money to a scammer on Snapchat?

Contact your bank immediately and report the fraud. Ask them to attempt to recall the payment and to assess a reimbursement claim: an eligible Faster Payments or CHAPS transfer sent on or after 7 October 2024 falls under the mandatory APP reimbursement rules, with a 13-month claim window, an £85,000 cap, and a possible excess of up to £100 that cannot be charged to a consumer the firm assesses as vulnerable. Report the scam to Report Fraud (0300 123 2040 in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland) or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. Report the Snapchat account to Snapchat itself. If you sent money via gift cards or cryptocurrency, report it to the platform where you bought them.
